ShareCommentary: Remote work changed everything for me. Three years in, I'm more productive than I've ever been in an office. The key isn't discipline — it's intentional structure. Fixed deep work blocks. No Slack before 11am. Walking meetings for calls that don't need a screen. What's your non-negotiable remote work habit?

Hot take: most AI features shipped in 2024 are solutions looking for problems. The ones that stick will be invisible — embedded so naturally into workflows that users forget they're using AI at all. We're in the hype peak. The interesting work starts when the hype fades.

Just finished leading my first team migration from a monolith to microservices. Lessons learned the hard way: 1) Start with the seams that already exist, don't invent new ones. 2) Strangler fig pattern actually works. 3) Distributed tracing is not optional. 4) Your team's cognitive load matters more than technical elegance.

The best engineers I've worked with all share one trait: they ask 'why' before 'how'. Not in an annoying way — in a way that clarifies assumptions and saves weeks of building the wrong thing. Curiosity as a professional skill is underrated.

Six months using vector databases in production. Thoughts: pgvector for most use cases (you already have Postgres), Pinecone when you need managed scale, Qdrant when you need filtering performance. The 'best' vector DB is the one your team can operate. Operational simplicity beats benchmark numbers.

We shipped RAG to production last quarter. What nobody tells you: the retrieval quality matters 10x more than the LLM choice. Swap GPT-4 for Claude — marginal difference. Fix chunking strategy and reranker — night and day. Invest in eval before you invest in model upgrades.
Career advice I wish I had at 25: your network is not the people who can give you a job. It's the people who will tell you the truth about your work. Find those people and hold onto them.

Finished reading 'Thinking in Systems' by Donella Meadows. Changed how I debug production issues. Every incident is a systems problem, not a people problem. Feedback loops, delays, and stocks explain almost every engineering failure I've seen.

PostgreSQL is the most underrated piece of infrastructure in the modern stack. Full-text search, JSONB, window functions, now vector similarity — it keeps eating use cases that used to require separate specialized databases. Boring? Yes. That's the point.

Interviewing engineers in 2024: I care less about LeetCode performance and more about how someone thinks through system design under ambiguity. Give me someone who asks great clarifying questions over someone who recites perfect solutions to rehearsed problems.

Three years as an IC, two as a tech lead, one as an engineering manager. Going back to IC was the best career decision I made. Some people are wired to build. Know which one you are before the title starts making decisions for you.

On async-first communication: our team removed all standing meetings except one weekly sync. Replaced them with well-structured Notion docs and Loom videos. Velocity increased 30%. More importantly, everyone gets to do their best thinking without constant interruption.

The hardest part of building with LLMs isn't the models. It's evaluation. How do you know if your prompt change made things better or worse? Invest in evals before you invest in anything else. Golden dataset. Automated scoring. Regression tests. Boring but essential.

India's tech ecosystem in 2024 is genuinely exciting. The quality of engineering talent, the density of ambitious founders, the appetite for hard problems — it's a different energy than five years ago. Proud to be building here.
Unpopular opinion: code reviews are primarily a knowledge transfer tool, not a quality gate. The real value is two engineers understanding the same code. The bugs you catch are a bonus.
Just crossed 1,000 GitHub contributions this year. Not a flex — a reminder that compound interest applies to skills too. Small consistent reps beat periodic heroics every time.

The secret to shipping fast: ruthless scope reduction, not heroic effort. Every feature you don't build is a bug you don't fix, a test you don't write, a concept you don't have to explain. The fastest path to done is a smaller done.
Started learning Rust last month. Coming from Python and Go, the borrow checker felt like a prison. Three weeks later, it feels like a safety net. Paradigm shifts take discomfort first.

2023 reflection: the best technical decision we made was choosing boring technology. SQLite for the job queue. Redis for caching. Postgres for everything else. Zero Kubernetes. Zero incidents from infrastructure complexity. Boring is a feature.
Year end advice: write down three things your team did well this year before you write down what to improve. Humans (and teams) are wired for negativity. Counter it intentionally.
